Skewed means tilted, pulled, or distorted in one direction — away from what would be straight, balanced, or fair. Think of it as the opposite of "even" or "neutral." Something skewed has been pushed off-centre, and the push is not random — it consistently leans one particular way.

The word is used in three main contexts: physical objects, general ideas and information, and statistics. All three share the same soul: asymmetry and lean.

When a physical object is skewed, it is at an angle or twisted out of its proper alignment. It's not straight; it's crooked.

Examples:

  • A picture frame on a wall that hangs slightly tilted is skewed.
  • If you park a car at an angle instead of straight in its spot, it's skewed.
  • Teeth that grow at an angle instead of straight are skewed.

This is the most literal sense — something that should be straight or properly aligned, but isn't.
2. General / Figurative Meaning (The Most Common Use)

This is where the word appears most often in everyday life. When information, results, a sample, a report, an opinion, or a perspective is described as skewed, it means it has been distorted or pulled in one direction — it doesn't represent reality fairly and evenly. It leans too much toward one side.

This distortion can happen in two ways:

  • Unintentionally — through a flawed process or incomplete information
  • Intentionally — when someone deliberately twists information to serve a purpose

Examples to make this crystal clear:

"The survey results were skewed because only young people responded."

Here, the survey should represent people of all ages. But because only young people filled it out, the results lean heavily toward young people's views. They don't represent the full picture. The results are distorted — they're skewed.

"His view of the city is skewed — he only visited the wealthy neighbourhoods."

He didn't see the whole city. His impression is tilted toward one kind of experience. It's not a balanced or complete view.

"The media coverage was skewed in favour of one political party."

The reporting didn't treat both sides equally. It was biased — leaning toward one party more than the other.

"Her judgment was skewed by her personal feelings for him."

Her emotions distorted her thinking. Instead of judging the situation fairly, she was pulled in a particular direction by how she felt.

The key idea here: Something skewed is not simply wrong — it is systematically biased in a direction. A broken clock is wrong. A clock that always runs 10 minutes fast is skewed — it has a consistent, directional error.

In mathematics and statistics, skewed has a precise technical meaning, though it rests on the same idea of imbalance.

Imagine you've collected a large amount of data — say, the monthly salaries of 1,000 people — and you plot them on a graph. If the data were perfectly balanced, the graph would look like a smooth hill with both sides equal (this is called a "normal" or "symmetrical" distribution). But real-world data often isn't like that. The hill is lopsided. That lopsidedness is called skew, and the distribution is called skewed.

There are two directions it can lean:

Right-skewed (Positively skewed)

Most values are clustered on the lower end, but there's a long tail stretching far out to the right (toward higher values).

Example: Income in a country. Most people earn moderate or low incomes, clustering together on the lower end of the graph. But a small number of extremely wealthy people earn millions — they create a long tail stretching to the right. The graph is not a symmetric hill; it has a heavy left side and a long, thin right tail. This is a right-skewed distribution.

Left-skewed (Negatively skewed)

Most values are clustered on the higher end, but there's a long tail stretching far out to the left (toward lower values).

Example: The age at which people die in a country with good healthcare. Most people live into old age — they cluster at the higher end (70s, 80s, 90s). But a smaller number of people die young (accidents, illness in childhood), pulling the tail to the left. This is a left-skewed distribution.

Why does it matter? A skewed distribution means the average (mean) can be misleading. In a right-skewed income distribution, the average income might be ₹80,000/month — but most people actually earn far less. The average got pulled upward by a few billionaires. The skew distorts what "typical" looks like.

1. Skewed implies a direction, not just error.
Something skewed doesn't just deviate from the truth randomly — it deviates consistently toward one side. This directional lean is what distinguishes "skewed" from words like "wrong" or "inaccurate."

2. Skewed doesn't always mean dishonest.
A skewed sample or skewed data can result from an honest mistake in how the data was collected — not from anyone trying to deceive. For example, if you survey people about internet usage but only survey them online, you've automatically excluded people who don't use the internet. The results are skewed, but not because anyone lied.

3. Skewed often implies "it should be balanced."
When you call something skewed, there's usually an implied standard of fairness or neutrality that it has failed to meet. You wouldn't call a one-sided personal diary "skewed" — you'd expect it to be personal. But a news report should be balanced, so a biased news report is rightly called skewed.

4. Degree matters.
Something can be slightly skewed or heavily/severely skewed. The more extreme the lean, the more misleading or distorted the picture becomes.

• skewed data — data that doesn't represent reality fairly
  • skewed results — findings that have been distorted by bias or flaws
  • skewed sample — a group studied that doesn't fairly represent the larger population
  • skewed perception / view / perspective — a way of seeing things that's been distorted
  • skewed distribution — statistical data that leans to one side
  • skewed towards / in favour of — leaning in a specific direction ("The funding is skewed towards urban areas.")
  • skewed by — distorted because of something ("The findings were skewed by the small sample size.")

Whenever you see the word skewed, ask yourself: What should be straight, balanced, or even here — and in which direction is it leaning instead?

A skewed picture frame leans left instead of hanging straight.
A skewed survey leans toward one group instead of representing everyone.
A skewed income distribution leans toward the many low earners with a tail toward the few ultra-rich.

In every case, something has been pulled away from balance — consistently, in one direction. That pull is what "skewed" names.
